prompt: On live traffic, which criterion can a judge NOT grade?

choices.text: Relevance, which needs the customer's own rating
choices.why: Relevance needs only the question and the reply, both in the trace.

choices.text: Correctness, which needs an expected answer
choices.why: Right. A customer's question comes with no answer key.

choices.text: Faithfulness, which needs the original documents
choices.why: The sources the model was given are recoverable from the trace.

choices.text: Tone, which needs a second judge to agree with the first
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson asks for a second judge.

prompt: Why does judge.py ask for one criterion per call rather than all of them at once?

choices.text: The judge model refuses prompts with more than one rubric
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: One call per criterion is cheaper than one call for all
choices.why: It repeats the reply and sources each time, so it costs more.

choices.text: JSON output has room for one field only
choices.why: The verdict already has three fields.

choices.text: Each verdict is then separate, with its own span and price
choices.why: Right. A criterion can be sampled, priced and compared on its own.

prompt: The judge failed the return-postage reply on faithfulness. What was wrong with its verdict?

choices.text: Nothing: verdict and reason were both right
choices.why: The reason said the reply does not state that the customer pays, which is exactly what it states.

choices.text: The verdict was right and the reason wrong
choices.why: Right. A verdict is only as useful as the reason somebody reads beside it.

choices.text: The verdict was wrong: the reply is faithful
choices.why: It contradicts its source, which says returns are free.

choices.text: The judge returned no verdict
choices.why: It returned fail, in the shape asked for.

prompt: Of the 88 refusals in the week, how many did the judge pass for relevance?
Graded on every reply of the week, what share passed relevance under release 2026.10.1?

choices.why: That is the old release.
That is the uniform tenth's estimate.
Right: 48 of 141.

choices.text: about 70%
choices.why: Neither release is near 70% by this judge.

prompt: Which are reasons the lesson gives for grading a sample rather than everything? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Every judgement is a model call with its own price
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The judge reads what customers typed, so fewer copies go to fewer places
choices.why: Right. Lesson 2's rules apply to the judge too.

choices.text: A judge graded on everything gives a less accurate rate
choices.why: Grading everything gives the narrowest interval there is.

choices.text: Traces older than a day cannot be graded
choices.why: The lesson grades a whole week.

prompt: Which replies are chosen decides whether a rate is unbiased; how many decides how ___ it is.
Why does sample.uniform choose by a hash of the trace id instead of a random number?

choices.text: Hashing is faster than any random generator
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given.

choices.text: So a rerun picks the same replies
choices.why: Right. Two people grading the 10% sample grade the same thing.

choices.text: A random number would pick the bad replies more often
choices.why: A random choice is unbiased too; it is just not repeatable.

choices.text: The trace id says which release answered
choices.why: The release is an attribute; the id carries nothing.

prompt: The stratified sample said 46.7% for release 2026.09.4, against the week's 43.3%. Why higher?

choices.text: Order requests were half the sample and a quarter of the week
choices.why: Right. This judge passes them more often, and nothing weighted them back.

choices.text: Thirty replies are too few to say anything
choices.why: Sixty per release is a usable sample; the error is in the design.

choices.text: The random seed chose the best replies
choices.why: A seed does not favour good replies.

choices.text: The judge has a rule that favours order requests
choices.why: It applies the same rubric to both; it happens to pass them more.

prompt: What is a targeted sample's pass rate good for?

choices.text: Comparing quality between two releases
choices.why: It measures the sampling rule, not the week.

choices.text: The quality number on the dashboard
choices.why: That is exactly where it must never go.

choices.text: Nothing as an estimate
choices.why: Right. Its use is the replies it finds, to read and turn into test cases.

choices.text: Setting the judge's threshold for the next week
choices.why: Thresholds are not tuned on a biased sample.

prompt: Match each sampling rule to what it is for.

pairs.right: a small group that matters on its own
a reading list of likely failures

prompt: How many replies of the week did the targeted sample grade?
What halves the error of a sampled pass rate?

choices.text: Twice as many replies graded
choices.why: Twice the sample cuts the error by about 30%.

choices.text: Twice as much traffic to sample from
choices.why: The size of the traffic does not enter.

choices.text: A judge twice as expensive
choices.why: Price has nothing to do with sampling error.

choices.text: Four times as many replies graded
choices.why: Right. The error falls with the square root of the sample.

prompt: Over the whole week the intervals were 35.2–51.7% and 26.7–42.2%. What is the honest report?

choices.text: The release made relevance worse by 9.3 points
choices.why: The difference of the estimates is not shown by intervals that overlap.

choices.text: No change, since the intervals overlap
choices.why: Overlap means the week cannot tell, not that nothing changed.

choices.text: The release improved relevance at the upper end
choices.why: An interval is not a range of outcomes that happened.

choices.text: Probably worse, not shown even by every reply
choices.why: Right. The week is the limit, not the sample.

prompt: A product has a million replies a week, another ten thousand. Each grades 400. Which rate is surer?

choices.text: Neither: both are known to about ±4.5 points
choices.why: Right. The number graded decides it.

choices.text: The million, because its sample is drawn from more data
choices.why: The traffic's size does not enter while the sample is a small part of it.

choices.text: The ten thousand, because 400 is a larger share of it
choices.why: 4% is still a small share; the gain is negligible.

choices.text: Neither, without grading everything
choices.why: That is what an interval is for.

prompt: For a pass rate of 70% on 100 replies, how many points either side is the 95% half-width, rounded to one decimal?
Where did the lesson get the price of grading from?

choices.text: An estimate from the length of each reply
choices.why: The tokens are measured, not estimated.

choices.text: The provider's monthly invoice for the lab
choices.why: The lab has no invoice; the spans carry the tokens.

choices.text: The judge's own spans, priced by costs.py
choices.why: Right. Grading is priced like serving.

choices.text: A table of fixed prices per criterion
choices.why: Prices are per token, by model and date.

prompt: What is the cheapest saving the lesson names for relevance calls?

choices.text: Grading relevance only on weekdays
choices.why: That biases the sample.

choices.text: Sending only what the rubric reads
choices.why: Right. The relevance rubric never asks about the sources, which travel anyway.

choices.text: Asking for a shorter reason in the verdict
choices.why: Output is a small part of the judge's tokens.

choices.text: Grading with a model as large as the assistant's
choices.why: Here the judge already is the assistant's model, and it cost more per call than a reply.

prompt: One judgement cost 0.00060674 dollars and one request 0.00046118. One judgement is what percentage of a request's cost, to the nearest whole number?
Why should a judge's spans carry a feature of their own, such as evaluation?

choices.text: So the judge is billed to a separate account
choices.why: The point is visibility, not billing.

choices.text: So that grading shows up as its own line of cost
choices.why: Right. A cost nobody sees grows without a decision.

choices.text: So the judge stops grading its own replies
choices.why: The judge never grades itself here.

choices.text: So the sampling rate is set from the dashboard
choices.why: A feature label sets nothing.

prompt: Order these policies from most to least costly in judge calls for this week.
A team wants to know whether a feature with 2% of traffic got worse. Which sample fits?

choices.text: A uniform tenth of all traffic
choices.why: It would hold very few of that feature's replies.

choices.text: Every reply of the week that got a thumbs down
choices.why: That finds failures; it does not estimate a rate.

choices.text: Stratified, with enough of that feature
choices.why: Right. And reweighted if it is ever combined into a total.

choices.text: The first hundred replies of Monday
choices.why: A corner of the week, not the feature.

prompt: Why does grade_sample.py write the sampling rule beside every verdict in verdicts.jsonl?

choices.text: So nobody later averages two kinds of sample
choices.why: Right. A targeted rate mixed with a uniform one estimates nothing.

choices.text: So that the judge reads it and grades accordingly
choices.why: The judge never sees verdicts.jsonl.

choices.text: Because the Wilson interval needs it to run
choices.why: Wilson needs only passed and graded.

choices.text: To price each verdict at its own sampling rate
choices.why: Price comes from tokens.

prompt: How many judge calls did the whole lesson make, from the cost capture?
